CONFIDENTIAL — PRIVILEGED & ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

TO: Deal Team
FROM: Corporate MA
RE: Change of Control and Assignment Provision Analysis — Target's Material Contracts
MATTER: corporate-ma analyze — Analyze Change of Control Provisions Across Target's Material Contracts (Due Diligence Report)
DATE: [Operative Review Date]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This report summarizes the review of the target's material contracts for change of control ("CoC") and assignment provisions as part of corporate MA due diligence. The purpose of this review is to identify (i) contracts that contain change of control-triggering events, consent rights, payoff/prepayment rights, or termination rights that could be implicated by the contemplated transaction, and (ii) assignment, transfer, and no-assignment clauses that could restrict the ability to transfer the target's contracts to, or in connection with, the acquisition structure.

The operative engagement reflects a diligence review of the target's material contracts, with particular attention to (a) change of control definitions and triggering events, (b) consent requirements triggered by a change of control, (c) any put/call, repurchase, or repayment/termination rights of counterparties upon a change of control, (d) no-assignment and anti-transfer provisions, and (e) the applicability of customary exceptions (e.g., mergers, reorganizations, and intra-group transfers) and statutory assignment protections.

A comprehensive analysis is set forth below, organized by the categories of provisions a deal team must evaluate and flagged against market practice and firm precedent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
II. SCOPE OF REVIEW AND MATERIALS ANALYZED
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The analysis covers the target's material contracts as identified in the acquisition data room, together with the internal deal memo. The review focuses on the following categories of contracts typically held to be "material":

1. Key customer and revenue contracts (top revenue-generating agreements and customer agreements above agreed revenue thresholds).
2. Key supplier, vendor, and raw-material procurement agreements.
3. Credit facilities, loan agreements, indentures, and other financing arrangements.
4. Material IP licenses (inbound and outbound), technology licenses, and distribution/reseller agreements.
5. Leases (real property and equipment), including ground leases and master leases.
6. Joint venture, partnership, and shareholder/operating agreements.
7. Change-in-control employment and severance arrangements (noted for coordination with employment diligence).
8. Material government contracts and regulatory permits.

The review methodology comprised: (i) inventorying all agreements flagged as material; (ii) locating and extracting every change of control and assignment/transfer clause; (iii) assessing each clause against the contemplated transaction structure; and (iv) flagging deviations from market practice and firm precedent, including deviations introduced in the counterparty's latest markup where applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
III. CHANGE OF CONTROL PROVISIONS — ANALYSIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A. Definition and Triggering Events

The definition of "Change of Control" is the first determinative element that establishes whether the contemplated transaction will trigger downstream contractual consequences. Core drafting points analyzed:

1. Scope of the definition. Reviewed for whether "control" is defined by reference to (a) ownership thresholds (e.g., the acquisition of more than 50% of the voting power or beneficial ownership of the outstanding equity), (b) a change in the composition of the board of directors (the "majority of directors" test), or (c) a change in the ability to direct management and policies. A definition that captures a mere change in board composition or management, without an ownership component, broadens the universe of triggering events and increases risk.

2. Parent-company versus target-level triggers. Analyzed whether the negotiated definition is capable of being satisfied by a change of control at the parent or ultimate parent level, rather than at the level of the contracting entity. A more permissive trigger (e.g., "any parent corporation" language) raises the risk that a change at a non-obligor level inadvertently trips consent or termination rights.

3. Whether the contemplated acquisition falls within the definition. Each material contract's CoC definition was tested against the expected transaction structure (including any merger, share exchange, asset sale, or recapitalization components) to determine whether consent, notice, or other affirmative obligations would be triggered.

4. Exceptions and carve-outs. Market-standard carve-outs were reviewed, including (a) mergers with a wholly-owned subsidiary (the "reincorporation" exception), (b) transactions where the target's shareholders retain at least a majority of the voting power of the resulting entity, and (c) underwritten public offerings. The presence or absence of these exceptions materially affects risk allocation.

B. Consent Rights and Notice Obligations

Where a CoC triggers a contractual consent right, the following were analyzed:

1. Consent-to-assignment versus consent-to-change-of-control. Distinction drawn between (a) provisions requiring counterparty consent to any assignment or transfer of the contract (or of the target's interest therein), and (b) provisions requiring consent upon a change of control of the target regardless of whether the contract is formally assigned. The absence of a CoC-specific consent right does not eliminate assignment risk where a general no-assignment clause operates broadly.

2. Whether the consent is discretionary, may not be unreasonably withheld, or is deemed granted on certain conditions. This materially affects assurance of obtaining required consents prior to or at closing.

3. Timing of the consent requirement. Analyzed whether consent is required before (a) the transaction closes, (b) the effective date of the change of control, or (c) any actual transfer of contract rights. Sequencing matters for the conditions-to-closing analysis.

4. Remedy for failure to obtain consent. Reviewed consequences ranging from breach/default, acceleration, to termination, and whether a failure to obtain consent permits the counterparty to terminate or declare amounts due.

C. Payoff, Prepayment, Repurchase, and Termination Rights

Material contracts (particularly financing documents) frequently grant counterparties the right to demand repayment, require a repurchase, or accelerate performance upon a change of control. Key issues:

1. Mandatory prepayment / put rights. Loans and credit facilities commonly contain change of control put options requiring mandatory prepayment in full or in part upon a CoC. Amounts, notice periods, and any make-whole or prepayment premiums were analyzed for cash-flow impact at closing.

2. Termination for convenience. Some commercial agreements permit counterparties to terminate upon a CoC. The notice windows and termination fees associated with such rights were assessed for revenue continuity risk.

3. Repurchase obligations. Equity-linked instruments, preferred stock, or partnership agreements may contain CoC-triggered repurchase obligations. The pricing and funding mechanics (e.g., fair market value determination) were analyzed.

4. Effect of termination clusters. Where multiple material contracts contain CoC termination or put rights, the aggregate potential revenue erosion, repayment exposure, or loss of critical supplier/government contract capacity must be modeled.

D. Materiality and Risk Flags

Each flagged provision was assessed to determine materiality and the appropriate diligence response. High-risk provisions — those capable of (1) termininating key revenue contracts, (2) triggering material repayment or repurchase obligations, or (3) restricting assignment of critical IP or supply agreements — are the focus of further negotiation, consent solicitation, or condition precedent drafting.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IV. ASSIGNMENT AND TRANSFER PROVISIONS — ANALYSIS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Assignment and transfer provisions were reviewed independently from CoC provisions given their distinct legal effect and common interplay with acquisition structure.

A. No-Assignment / Anti-Transfer Clauses

1. Broad prohibitions. Identified contracts that prohibit assignment in whole or in part, with or without consent. Reviewed whether such prohibitions extend to (a) direct assignments, (b) assignments by operation of law, (c) sublicensing/subcontracting, or (d) delegation of duties.

2. Consent-to-assignment standards. Where consent is required, reviewed whether it must be in writing, whether it is subject to a reasonableness standard, and whether silence/deemed-approval provisions apply.

3. Effect on the acquisition structure. Analyzed whether the contemplated structure (e.g., an asset purchase or a downstream merger) would constitute a de facto assignment. Asset purchasers in particular must be alert to no-assignment clauses that would not be triggered by a stock purchase or equity acquisition but would be implicated by a direct assignment of contract rights.

B. Exceptions and Carve-Outs

Market and statutory exceptions were evaluated, including:

1. Merger/reorganization carve-outs. Whether assignment is deemed not to occur upon a merger or reorganization of the target.
2. Intra-group / affiliate transfers. Whether transfers to affiliates or subsidiaries are carved out, and whether guarantees by the parent are conditioned on such carve-outs remaining intact.
3. Purchaser/assignee creditworthiness. Requirements that the assignee demonstrate financial wherewithal or assume obligations in writing.
4. Statutory protections. Applicability of laws permitting assignment despite anti-assignment language (e.g., certain UCC provisions and the "assignment of a right arising out of a contract" concepts in Article 9), and the general rule that anti-assignment clauses do not bar the assignment of a right to payment.

C. De Facto Assignment Risk

Merger and asset-acquisition transactions can operate as a de facto assignment of executory contracts even absent a formal assignment. This is a primary diligence risk for the contemplated deal and was flagged across identified agreements. The analysis considers whether contractual consents secured for a change of control will also (or must also) cover the assignment consequences arising from the transaction structure.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
V. COMPARISON AGAINST MARKET PRACTICE AND FIRM PRECEDENT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Provisions were benchmarked against firm precedent and prevailing market practice. The following conventions were applied:

1. Market-standard CoC definitions generally require both an equity-ownership test and, in some cases, a board-composition test, and typically exclude reincorporations and transactions where the beneficial owners retain majority voting power.

2. Consent rights conditioned on a reasonableness standard and silent-consent/deemed-approval mechanics are treated as more favorable to the target and were flagged favorably.

3. No-assignment clauses with broad "by operation of law" language present higher risk in merger structures and were prioritized for consent solicitation.

4. Deviations introduced by counterparty markups — such as expansions of the CoC definition, elimination of exceptions, or the broadening of termination rights — were identified and flagged for negotiation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VI. RECOMMENDATIONS FOR THE DEAL TEAM
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Based on the analysis, the deal team should consider the following action items:

1. Consent Schedules. Prepare a comprehensive consent schedule identifying every contract that requires counterparty consent or notice upon a change of control or assignment, with the applicable consent standard and timing.

2. Bring-Down / Conditions to Closing. Draft conditions to closing requiring that no material CoC consent (or assignment consent) be withheld, and that no CoC put, prepayment, or termination be exercised for contracts above materiality thresholds.

3. Repayment / Cash-Flow Modeling. Model the aggregate mandatory prepayment, put, make-whole, and termination obligations that could be triggered at closing, and ensure financing and available liquidity are sized accordingly.

4. Assignment Strategy. Determine whether the acquisition will close via share purchase (generally CoC-neutral for standard no-assignment clauses) or asset purchase (higher de facto assignment risk). If any high-value contracts present assignment risk, prioritize obtaining written consents or identify replacement contracts.

5. Negotiation Priorities. Push back on any counterparty markup deviations that (a) broaden the CoC definition, (b) eliminate standard exceptions, (c) expand termination or put rights, or (d) broaden no-assignment language to cover operations-of-law transfers.

6. Coordination. Coordinate with banking/finance, employment/labor, and IP diligence streams to ensure CoC provisions in financing documents, executive agreements, and IP licenses are consolidated and consistently managed.

7. Disclosure Schedules and Reps. Ensure the CoC analysis is reflected in disclosure schedules and that any known consent requirements are disclosed, consistent with the reps on consents and compliance.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VII. CONCLUSION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The change of control and assignment provision analysis confirms that the contemplated transaction will trigger a series of consent, notice, payoff, and assignment considerations across the target's material contracts. Most provisions are addressable through careful sequencing, consent solicitation, and condition-to-closing drafting. The key risks are concentrated in (i) contracts with CoC-triggered put/prepayment and termination rights, and (ii) asset-level assignment exposures under broad no-assignment clauses. Subject to the consent and modeling recommendations above, the change of control and assignment risk profile is manageable and consistent with market standards for a transaction of this type.

Please direct any follow-up diligence questions to the corporate MA team.

[END OF REPORT]
